## equal_weighted

Equal weight (1/N)

**Year:** —

**Origin:** A very old rule of thumb (it even appears in the Talmud). Its academic fame comes from DeMiguel, Garlappi and Uppal's 2009 paper "Optimal Versus Naive Diversification": most of 14 optimisation models failed to beat 1/N consistently out of sample.

**Core idea:** Gives every asset the same share; makes no forecasts at all.

**How to read the results:** Treat it as the benchmark rather than a model. Read every other backtest against it: if a model cannot beat equal weight on a risk-adjusted basis (Sharpe), its extra complexity adds no value for these assets.

**Strength:** No estimation error, easy to understand, low trading costs.

**Caution:** Ignores risk: a very volatile asset gets the same share as a calm one and ends up carrying most of the risk.

## inverse_volatility

Inverse-volatility weighting

**Year:** 1990s

**Origin:** A long-standing practitioner rule; considered the simplest form of risk parity, one that ignores correlations.

**Core idea:** Each asset's share is inversely proportional to its volatility: calmer assets get more.

**How to read the results:** The largest weight sits in the calmest asset. Check how much volatility drops versus equal weight and compare it with how much return you give up.

**Strength:** Simple and stable; only volatilities are estimated, no return forecasts needed.

**Caution:** Ignores correlations; two very similar calm assets can jointly end up overweight.

## min_variance

Minimum variance (Markowitz)

**Year:** 1952

**Origin:** Harry Markowitz, "Portfolio Selection" (Journal of Finance, 1952), the start of modern portfolio theory; Markowitz won the 1990 Nobel Prize. This end point, which needs no return forecasts, regained popularity through Clarke, de Silva and Thorley (2006).

**Core idea:** Uses volatilities and co-movements (covariance) to find the mix with the lowest total volatility.

**How to read the results:** Weights pile into low-volatility assets that move little with the others. A low 'effective number of assets' means the portfolio is concentrated. In backtests it usually shows one of the shallowest drawdowns but below-average returns.

**Strength:** Relatively robust to estimation error because it uses no return forecasts.

**Caution:** Can concentrate in a few calm assets; low risk may also mean low return.

## max_sharpe

Maximum Sharpe ratio

**Year:** 1958 / 1966

**Origin:** James Tobin's separation theorem (1958) and William Sharpe's reward-to-variability ratio (1966). It is the 'tangency portfolio' of Markowitz's efficient frontier. Sharpe shared the 1990 Nobel Prize.

**Core idea:** Finds the mix with the highest expected return per unit of risk (Sharpe ratio).

**How to read the results:** It loads up on the past winners. Check how much the weights move when you change the start date. Even if it looks great in a backtest, that may not repeat next period.

**Strength:** In theory the most efficient risk/return trade-off; strongest when your return forecasts are good.

**Caution:** Highly sensitive to past average returns; small data changes swing the weights sharply (Michaud called it 'error maximisation' in 1989).

## max_sharpe_shrunk

Max Sharpe with shrunk expected returns and Ledoit-Wolf covariance

**Year:** 1986 / 2004

**Origin:** James-Stein-type shrinkage of means (Jorion, 1986) and Ledoit and Wolf's covariance shrinkage estimator (2004).

**Core idea:** A more cautious max-Sharpe that pulls extreme estimates towards the average.

**How to read the results:** Compare it side by side with classic max-Sharpe: a more balanced mix means shrinkage is dampening estimation error. If it delivers similar backtest returns with shallower drawdowns, prefer it.

**Strength:** More stable than max-Sharpe; lower overfitting risk.

**Caution:** Still relies on past returns; shrinkage reduces error but does not remove it.

## min_cvar

Minimum CVaR (95%)

**Year:** 2000

**Origin:** R. Tyrrell Rockafellar and Stanislav Uryasev, "Optimization of Conditional Value-at-Risk" (2000), which made CVaR optimisable with linear programming. Basel III market-risk rules later moved to the same idea (Expected Shortfall).

**Core idea:** Minimises the average loss on the worst 5% of days (CVaR 95%).

**How to read the results:** Its 'CVaR 95%' in the backtest should be low. If its weights resemble min-variance, tail losses in the data are limited; if they differ a lot, some assets carry more tail risk than their volatility suggests.

**Strength:** Directly targets tail risk, the days of sharp falls.

**Caution:** Relies on a few bad days; results can be unstable with short histories.

## max_sortino

Maximum Sortino ratio

**Year:** 1991 / 1994

**Origin:** Frank Sortino; Sortino & van der Meer (1991) and Sortino & Price (1994). Built on the idea that investors only dislike downside swings.

**Core idea:** Maximises return per unit of downside volatility only.

**How to read the results:** Similar to max-Sharpe but does not penalise upside jumps, so it may favour assets with positive skew. Check the Sortino column in the backtest.

**Strength:** Focuses on the risk investors actually fear: losses.

**Caution:** Like max-Sharpe, highly sensitive to past returns.

## min_cdar

Minimum CDaR (drawdown risk)

**Year:** 2003

**Origin:** Alexei Chekhlov, Stanislav Uryasev and Michael Zabarankin, "Drawdown Measure in Portfolio Optimization" (2003/2005).

**Core idea:** Minimises the average of the worst drawdowns from previous peaks.

**How to read the results:** Look at 'Max drawdown' and the drawdown chart: falls should be shallower and shorter. Most relevant for investors who care about recovery time.

**Strength:** The risk measure closest to investor psychology: 'how far, and for how long, am I below my peak?'

**Caution:** Depends on the order of past drawdown episodes; a future crisis may hit different assets.

## min_max_drawdown

Minimum max drawdown

**Year:** 2003

**Origin:** The extreme case of Chekhlov, Uryasev and Zabarankin's drawdown-measure family.

**Core idea:** Minimises the single deepest historical drawdown.

**How to read the results:** The result is shaped largely by one crisis episode. Move the start date so that crisis is excluded and see how much the weights change.

**Strength:** Targets the most direct protection against the worst scenario.

**Caution:** Because it is tuned to one event, it is among the least stable risk models.

## max_diversification

Maximum diversification ratio

**Year:** 2008

**Origin:** Yves Choueifaty and Yves Coignard, "Toward Maximum Diversification" (Journal of Portfolio Management, 2008); used commercially by TOBAM.

**Core idea:** Maximises the diversification ratio (weighted sum of asset risks divided by portfolio risk).

**How to read the results:** It favours the least similar assets. In the correlation heat map (Data tab) the low-correlation assets should be the ones it overweights.

**Strength:** Uses no return forecasts; targets genuine diversification directly.

**Caution:** Correlations rise in crises, so diversification may shrink just when you need it most.

## dro_cvar

Distributionally robust CVaR (Wasserstein)

**Year:** 2018

**Origin:** Peyman Mohajerin Esfahani and Daniel Kuhn, distributionally robust optimisation with the Wasserstein metric (Mathematical Programming, 2018).

**Core idea:** Minimises CVaR under the worst of all distributions 'close' to the historical data.

**How to read the results:** Compare it with min-CVaR: more balanced weights show the model is not over-trusting history. As the uncertainty radius grows it approaches equal weight.

**Strength:** Assumes the data will not perfectly reflect the future; cautious against surprises.

**Caution:** Computationally heavy; may be overly cautious and give up too much return.

## risk_parity

Risk parity (equal risk contribution, variance)

**Year:** 1996 / 2005

**Origin:** Bridgewater's All Weather fund (Ray Dalio, 1996) and Edward Qian, who coined the term (PanAgora, 2005). Maillard, Roncalli and Teïletche (2010) formalised its properties.

**Core idea:** Splits risk, not capital, equally: every asset contributes the same to total risk.

**How to read the results:** Weights are unequal, yet the 'Risk source' line in the comments should show no single dominant asset. Calm assets receive more capital.

**Strength:** Needs no return forecasts; usually stays balanced through crises.

**Caution:** Allocates a lot of capital to calm assets; if they fall together the impact is large.

## risk_parity_cvar

Risk parity (CVaR)

**Year:** 2010s

**Origin:** A generalisation of risk parity to tail-risk measures (e.g. Boudt, Carl and Peterson, 2013).

**Core idea:** Equalises each asset's contribution to tail risk (CVaR).

**How to read the results:** Look at the difference from variance-based risk parity: assets with sudden sharp falls should get less here.

**Strength:** Makes no normal-distribution assumption; accounts for sharp falls directly.

**Caution:** Tail estimates rest on few observations; can be unstable with short data.

## hrp

Hierarchical risk parity (López de Prado)

**Year:** 2016

**Origin:** Marcos López de Prado, "Building Diversified Portfolios that Outperform Out of Sample" (Journal of Portfolio Management, 2016), bringing machine-learning clustering to portfolio construction.

**Core idea:** Clusters assets into a tree by similarity, then splits risk top-down along the branches.

**How to read the results:** Similar assets (e.g. stocks in the same sector) share their weight as a group. Weights should be fairly stable across periods; compare their variability with max-Sharpe.

**Strength:** Never inverts the covariance matrix; robust to estimation error and to many assets.

**Caution:** Can concentrate in the calm asset when volatilities differ a lot; the clustering method affects the result.

## hrp_cdar

HRP with the CDaR risk measure

**Year:** 2016+

**Origin:** HRP with drawdown risk (CDaR) instead of variance, generalised in skfolio and Riskfolio-Lib.

**Core idea:** Uses the HRP tree but splits risk by drawdown risk.

**How to read the results:** Compare with classic HRP: assets that stay below their peaks for long should get less here.

**Strength:** Combines HRP's robustness with a drawdown-focused risk measure.

**Caution:** Drawdown measures depend on the order of past crises.

## herc

Hierarchical equal risk contribution

**Year:** 2017

**Origin:** Thomas Raffinot, "Hierarchical Clustering-Based Asset Allocation" (2017) and HERC (2018).

**Core idea:** Identifies clusters first, gives each cluster an equal share of risk, then splits risk within clusters.

**How to read the results:** The number of clusters drives the result; with few assets a lone asset in its own cluster can get a large share. Check this in the weight chart.

**Strength:** Fixes HRP's 'split the tree in half' issue by using the actual cluster structure.

**Caution:** Results can swing sharply with few assets.

## nco

Nested clustered optimisation

**Year:** 2019

**Origin:** Marcos López de Prado, "A Robust Estimator of the Efficient Frontier" (2019) and "Machine Learning for Asset Managers" (2020).

**Core idea:** Optimises first within each cluster, then across clusters.

**How to read the results:** Shines with many assets (20+). With few assets, as here, don't be surprised if it resembles min-variance.

**Strength:** Limits how much noise in the covariance matrix can distort the optimisation.

**Caution:** Little extra benefit with few assets; unstable clustering means unstable results.

## schur

Schur complementary allocation (between HRP and min variance)

**Year:** 2024

**Origin:** Peter Cotton, "Schur Complementary Allocation" (2024), bridging HRP and Markowitz.

**Core idea:** Uses HRP's tree but keeps cross-cluster correlation information (via the Schur complement) when allocating.

**How to read the results:** Its weights usually land between HRP and min-variance; compare it side by side with both.

**Strength:** Keeps HRP's robustness while using correlation information better.

**Caution:** A new method; long-term independent testing is limited.

## stacking

Stacking: HRP + min var + risk parity + max diversification

**Year:** 1992

**Origin:** David Wolpert, "Stacked Generalization" (1992); adapted from machine learning to portfolios by skfolio.

**Core idea:** Treats the portfolios of several models (HRP, min-variance, risk parity, max diversification) as 'assets' and optimises across them.

**How to read the results:** Its result is a blend of the component models. If it doesn't beat their average in the backtest, the extra complexity isn't worth it.

**Strength:** Aims to balance out the mistakes of any single model.

**Caution:** Depends on its components and is slower to compute.

## riskfolio_hrp

Riskfolio-Lib HRP (Ward)

**Year:** 2016

**Origin:** Riskfolio-Lib's (Dany Cajas) implementation of López de Prado's HRP, using Ward linkage.

**Core idea:** Same idea as HRP with a different clustering (linkage) method.

**How to read the results:** Compare with skfolio's HRP; a large difference shows the result is sensitive to the clustering method.

**Strength:** Ward linkage tends to build more balanced, compact clusters.

**Caution:** HRP's limitations apply here as well.

## riskfolio_max_sharpe_cvar

Riskfolio-Lib max return/CVaR

**Year:** 2000+

**Origin:** Rockafellar-Uryasev CVaR used in a return/risk ratio; Riskfolio-Lib implementation.

**Core idea:** Maximises expected return divided by CVaR.

**How to read the results:** Unlike max-Sharpe it penalises sharp falls rather than volatility. If its weights resemble max-Sharpe, tail risk in the data is not pronounced.

**Strength:** Combines return seeking with tail-risk control.

**Caution:** Sensitive to past returns.

## riskfolio_min_cdar

Riskfolio-Lib minimum CDaR

**Year:** 2003

**Origin:** Riskfolio-Lib implementation of Chekhlov-Uryasev-Zabarankin CDaR.

**Core idea:** Same goal as min-CDaR with a different library and solver settings.

**How to read the results:** Should almost match skfolio's min-CDaR; any difference comes from solver precision.

**Strength:** Lets you cross-check the result with two independent implementations.

**Caution:** The usual drawdown-measure limitations apply.

## pypfopt_max_sharpe

PyPortfolioOpt max Sharpe (Ledoit-Wolf)

**Year:** 1966 / 2004

**Origin:** Sharpe ratio with Ledoit-Wolf covariance; PyPortfolioOpt (Robert Martin) implementation.

**Core idea:** Finds the max-Sharpe portfolio using a shrunk covariance.

**How to read the results:** Compare with skfolio's max-Sharpe; shrinkage smooths the covariance so weights may be slightly more balanced.

**Strength:** Slightly more stable than classic max-Sharpe.

**Caution:** Expected returns are still historical averages.

## pypfopt_cla_min_vol

PyPortfolioOpt Critical Line Algorithm minimum volatility

**Year:** 1956

**Origin:** Markowitz's Critical Line Algorithm (1956); open-source implementation by Bailey and López de Prado (2013).

**Core idea:** Finds the minimum-volatility portfolio with a dedicated algorithm that traces the whole efficient frontier exactly.

**How to read the results:** Should nearly match min-variance; read it as a cross-check of that result.

**Strength:** Exact and fast compared with general-purpose solvers.

**Caution:** Min-variance limitations apply.

## Black-Litterman

**Year:** 1990 / 1992

**Origin:** Fischer Black and Robert Litterman, Goldman Sachs (1990; Financial Analysts Journal, 1992), developed in response to Markowitz's extreme-weight problem.

**Core idea:** Blends a 'neutral' market expectation with your views, weighted by your confidence in them.

**How to read the results:** Compare the weights with and without views: the change is the impact of your views. Raising confidence (tau) gives your views more weight.

**Strength:** Brings personal views into the portfolio consistently and in moderation.

**Caution:** Only as good as your views; a wrong view, even in moderation, still pushes in the wrong direction.
